⚡ Energy finance is about architecture — building systems that investors and citizens can both trust. In 2024, global renewable investment reached USD 624 billion, yet less than 15 percent reached developing economies outside China — and only 2–3 percent to Africa. 

The task ahead is not just to mobilize more capital, but to unlocking opportunities for clean energy where the need and potential are greatest. That requires financial and institutional systems capable of structuring, verifying, and absorbing investments at scale.

At the 14th International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, leaders from across regions agreed: capital follows credibility. A few ways they converged on we can do this:

1️⃣ Build national financing ecosystems, not fragmented projects, that can enable bankability of projects.
Energy-efficiency funds in Kosovo, Jordan, and Moldova show these financial mechanisms. The key for bankability starts with structuring projects with clear revenue models, transparent governance, and measurable performance to minimize investor risk.

2️⃣ Aggregate small projects to match investor logic.
Commercial lenders seek diversification. Aggregating small clean-energy projects — solar rooftops, retrofits, micro-grids — into verified portfolios lowers risk premiums and opens new credit lines for municipalities and SMEs. Inclusion also remains the ultimate de-risking strategy, as funds led by women in risk-management roles have proven on average lower default rates.

3️⃣ Embed data integrity into all financial instruments as the foundation of credibility.
Accurate baselines, open performance data, and auditability are now prerequisites for green finance. In Africa, the @AFREC Energy Information System is helping lenders quantify risk and track national progress with greater confidence. Digital monitoring and AI-driven analytics can accelerate access to finance — but ensuring the datasets they are built on are equitable remains central.

The real measure of progress will be how fast we can turn global liquidity into local legitimacy — through institutions capable of absorbing, managing, and sustaining capital.

Hydrogen is not a standalone investment—it depends on water resources, land availability, and grid capacity. Not every country can or should pursue large-scale hydrogen. The right pathway depends on water availability, land constraints, energy access needs, and industrial priorities. 🔹 AI infrastructure must strengthen resilience, not compete with it. In water-stressed and capacity-constrained settings, unmanaged AI growth can privilege data centres over households, health services, and small businesses, deepening inequality.

If green hydrogen is the future, who gets to own that future?

By 2050, hydrogen is projected to supply around 12% of global energy demand, with demand rising to over 430 million tonnes. Yet around 83% of global hydrogen investment remains concentrated in Europe and China, even as many of the world's most competitive low-cost production sites are likely to emerge across Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East.

This raises a bigger development question: will countries become producers of green hydrogen, or creators of the industries, jobs, and value chains built around it?

This was a central theme from today's discussion at the University of Oxford on the UNDP -TIDE Centre, University of Oxford report Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human-Centred Framework.

While the opportunity is growing rapidly, delivery is still struggling to keep pace. By 2023, although 4.3 GW of global green hydrogen capacity had been announced, only 0.3 GW — around 7% — had actually been built. The constraint is no longer renewable potential alone. Increasingly, the barriers are governance, finance, infrastructure, and institutional readiness.

Three strategic priorities stand out:

🔹 From export commodities to integrated value chains. Hydrogen should be viewed not only as an export opportunity, but as an industrial strategy. The greatest development gains may come from local manufacturing, green fertilisers, and decarbonised industries — not raw hydrogen exports.

🔹 Jobs, skills, and national innovation systems. Chile aims to create over 100,000 jobs through its hydrogen strategy, while India targets around 500,000 jobs and 125 GW of renewable capacity by 2030. South Korea shows how coordinated ecosystems across research institutions, universities, and industry can transform hydrogen into a national innovation system.

🔹 Linking hydrogen finance and infrastructure with public value. The risk is that hydrogen projects become closed export enclaves — privately powered, externally financed, and weakly connected to domestic economies. South Africa's hydrogen strategy includes EU support for ports, railways, and pipeline infrastructure, while Brazil's Ceará Green Hydrogen Hub is anchoring around $7 billion in industrial and logistics investments.

The success of green hydrogen will not be measured by megawatts or export contracts alone. It will be measured by whether countries build capabilities, create decent jobs, safeguard resources, and advance shared prosperity.

The energy transition must, above all, serve people.

Today at the University of Cambridge, I had the pleasure of discussing how artificial intelligence, energy systems, and digital infrastructure are increasingly converging into the same transformation, reshaping economies, industrial systems, and development pathways simultaneously.
 
Throughout history, major energy transitions changed far more than how societies generated power.
 
And now we may be entering a new inflection point: planetary intelligence - the emergence of an intelligent layer across energy systems, digital infrastructure, finance, satellites, sensors, and public institutions.
 
Artificial intelligence is often described as something virtual. Yet it is becoming deeply physical. Some of the largest AI data centres now consume as much electricity as around 2 million households.
 
But perhaps the deeper question is this: Do we know yet whether AI will reduce inequality or deepen it?
 
The answer is, we do not know yet. What we do know is that behind every major technological shift lies a transformational opportunity.
 
Three opportunities particularly stood out during today’s discussion:
 
• Build AI infrastructure that strengthens energy systems rather than fragmenting them. Across Africa, data-centre demand could grow from around 0.4 GW today to between 1.5 and 2.2 GW by 2030, requiring an estimated $10–20 billion in investment. If planned strategically, this growth could help accelerate grid modernization, renewable integration, energy efficiency, and resilient infrastructure development.
 
• Turn renewable energy systems into intelligent systems. Renewable systems are becoming too large, decentralized, and dynamic to manage without advanced coordination. AI-enabled transmission management alone could unlock up to 175 GW of additional grid capacity from existing infrastructure.
 
• Build national digital-energy ecosystems and local value chains. Around $5.8 trillion is expected to flow into global grid infrastructure between 2026 and 2035, including roughly $700 billion in digital grid technologies. The deeper opportunity lies in building local industries, technical capabilities, services, software ecosystems, and new value chains around the transition itself.
 
Perhaps this is ultimately why the AI-energy transition matters for development.
 
Because energy innovation is never only about producing electricity differently. It is about reshaping how societies manage water, food systems, cities, industry, health, jobs, and resilience.

When planning ministries, utilities, finance ministries, and regulators work from the same models, coordination improves. Pipelines become clearer. Policy becomes more coherent. Finance becomes easier to mobilize. Modelling becomes a common language linking national plans, climate commitments, and investment decisions into one credible framework.
 
The conversations in Évian will shape the global energy agenda. But the deeper test is whether every country, not only the G7, can shape its own future with the same foresight. 
 
Energy modelling is no longer an add-on. It is strategic infrastructure. And it decides whether a country locks in vulnerability or builds lasting resilience.

The numbers tell a story that goes well beyond the remaining challenges.
Since the SDGs were adopted in 2015, the number of people living without electricity has fallen from 958 million to 655 million. Renewable energy has grown by 79% since 2013, now accounting for 18% of global final energy consumption and more than 30% of global electricity generation. Installed renewable energy capacity has more than doubled—from 248 watts per person in 2015 to 544 watts per person in 2024—while international public finance supporting clean energy in developing countries has increased from USD 14.3 billion to USD 24.6 billion.
 
Yet if we look beyond the numbers, an even more important story is emerging.
 
The world is not facing the same energy transition we imagined in 2015. Geopolitical uncertainty, shifting supply chains, climate risks and the rapid rise of AI are fundamentally reshaping energy systems. But these changes are also creating unprecedented incentives to accelerate the transition.

Polluting cooking costs the world more than US$2.4 trillion each year. Universal access would require around US$8 billion annually through 2030.
We are paying trillions to avoid investing billions.

Clean cooking requires more than distributing stoves. It needs fuels, finance, infrastructure, local businesses and services that households can depend on every day.

More than 120 clean cooking policies have been introduced across Africa over the past two years. Through Mission 300, its partnership with UNCDF and a portfolio reaching more than 2.5 million people, UNDP is helping turn that momentum into functioning markets and investable programmes.

The return is cleaner air, time returned to women and girls, stronger local businesses and more resilient economies.

The return is measured in lives saved, hours reclaimed by women and girls, businesses built and forests protected. At US$8 billion a year, the question is why we continue to pay US$2.4 trillion instead.

The world is planning for a surge in electricity demand. 

How can this be turned into an opportunity for energy security and socio-economic resilience?

Yesterday, UNDP joined the COP31 Türkiye –IEA–UN High-Level Energy Transition Solutions Dialogue at UN Headquarters. The IEA also released new analysis prepared for the COP31 discussions.

Its findings point to the scale of the opportunity. Electricity could cost-effectively meet 33% of global final energy use by 2035, up from 23% today, putting the proposed 35% goal within reach. In a faster electrification scenario, fuel-importing countries could cut their energy import bills by more than US$400 billion by 2035—reducing exposure to volatile fossil-fuel markets and strengthening energy security.

Accelerating electrification can create a broader development dividend. Investment in renewable energy, grids, storage and clean technologies can support green jobs, build domestic value chains and drive green industrialization, to power that businesses and communities need to grow.

But realizing this opportunity will require investment in generation and grids, while addressing the upfront costs that can prevent households and businesses from benefiting. Around 1.18 billion people still experience energy poverty, while Africa receives only 2% of global clean energy investment.

UNDP is supporting this effort alongside around 30 UN entities, with the aim of helping at least 100 countries build the policies and project pipelines needed to put finance to work.

The opportunity is not simply to electrify more of the global economy, but to use electrification to build more secure, resilient and inclusive economies. Which country, after Norway, had the highest share of electric cars in new car sales last year? Nepal, at 68%.

I opened with that question at today’s SDG7 Action Forum in New York. We often describe SDG7 through its gaps: 655 million people without electricity and two billion without clean cooking. But that account misses how quickly energy markets are changing.

Solar’s share of global electricity has risen from 1% to around 9% in a decade. Developing and emerging economies will account for 85% of electricity demand growth through 2035. Three priorities follow:

Build the systems around the power. Africa is heading for around 17 GW of new solar this year. Grids and storage must keep pace. In Mauritius, UNDP has supported smart-grid technology and 18 MW of battery storage.

Lower financing costs. The same solar project can face two to three times the cost of capital in many emerging economies. A one percentage point reduction could save US$150 billion a year.

Keep more value locally. Electricity should power farms, businesses, and industry. Yet of 16.6 million renewable energy jobs worldwide, only 344,000 are in Africa.

By 2030, how much of the transition’s value will stay in the countries producing its power?

Everyone is asking who will win the AI race. During yesterday’s IEEE Tech for Sustainability Summit in New York, I posed a different question: what does winning actually mean?

For me, the answer starts with energy.

AI could help unlock up to 175 GW of capacity from existing transmission lines. Across the Global South, companies are already using it for grid optimisation, smart metering, forecasting and industrial efficiency.

But the same technology can push in the opposite direction. AI is also making oil and gas exploration faster and cheaper, with recent modelling suggesting the resulting emissions could be 3.3 to 13.3 times larger than estimated 2025 data-centre emissions.

So the question is not whether AI is efficient. It is what AI is making more efficient.

This matters when 91% of new utility-scale renewable projects are already cheaper than the cheapest new fossil alternative. In Pakistan, low-cost solar imports helped avoid more than $12 billion in fuel imports. In Chile, financing for the 151 MW Calama wind farm was linked to emissions avoided through early coal retirement.

AI will add another major source of electricity demand. Whether that extends the age of energy addition or accelerates the transition will depend on choices around grids, finance, standards and public policy.

And who captures the value?

Middle-income countries generate more than 40% of ChatGPT traffic, yet middle- and low-income countries host only around 27% of shared data-centre facilities.

A sustainable AI framework must therefore ask what AI enables across the economy, where infrastructure is built, who owns the capabilities, and what countries gain in return.

Human intelligence created this wave. The task now is to decide where we direct it.
